data.title: How Victoria’s Secret CEO Hillary Super is reconnecting a storied brand with its customers
data.description: When Hillary Super became the CEO of Victoria’s Secret & Co. in 2024, she took on a difficult task: reconnecting the iconic lingerie company with a customer base it had been losing gradually for a decade.

data.title: Oil prices jump sharply, to nearly $110 per barrel
data.description: Oil prices jumped sharply Friday to their highest levels in weeks, as investors assessed the impact of both the Iran and Ukraine-Russia wars on global energy supplies. Brent crude oil spiked above $109 per barrel, its highest level since mid-September. The oil price benchmark — widely considered to be among the most important figures in global energy — was just a few cents away from its highest level in five months. U.S. crude oil, which also steers gas prices, rose to $100 per barrel. It was the first time West Texas Intermediate crude had crossed that threshold, closely watched by both traders and the public, since September. Friday’s price jumps will likely add to already elevated gasoline prices for U.S. consumers in coming days. As of Friday morning, regular gasoline averaged $4.32 per gallon nationwide. At midafternoon trading levels, oil prices were poised to gain about 5% over the course of the week. Diesel futures also jumped by more than 1% Friday. The cost of this commercial fuel critical for farming and other industrial sectors has risen even faster than regular gasoline in recent months. Stocks fell Friday, partly in response to the jump in energy prices. The S&P 500 fell more than 1% while the Nasdaq Composite sharply dropped 2% by midafternoon. The price of fuel around the world began its steady rise this spring, when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February, prompting the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But an escalation in the Russia-Ukraine war in recent months has caused an even more dramatic price spike for diesel. Russia has traditionally been one of the world’s largest diesel exporters. But attack by Ukrainian forces on its energy infrastructure has taken much of its refining capacity offline. Likewise, energy assets in Ukraine have been targeted by Russian strikes. As a result of the strikes, buyers of Russian diesel have been forced to look elsewhere for their fuel supplies. But there aren’t any clear opportunities to easily expand diesel production. Refineries in the U.S. and Europe are already running at nearly maximum capacity to churn out as much diesel fuel as possible. President Donald Trump is intensely focused on the high cost of diesel fuel because of its key role in driving up inflation -- a top issue for American voters in the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Trump has pressured U.S. allies to release some of their diesel and crude oil reserves, and he recently signed an order to ease regulations on the use of off-road “red dye” diesel. When neither of these actions resulted in a significant step down for diesel prices, Trump made the decision this month to ease U.S. sanctions on Russia. The goal was to allow Russian President Vladimir Putin to release some of Russia’s supplies to the global market. But the sanctions relief stunned world leaders and drew quick condemnation from U.S. lawmakers in both parties. While Trump has touted the deal with Putin as a way to lower prices, as of Friday, no actual Russian diesel had been identified as having reached the global market. Russia’s refining infrastructure has been badly damaged by Ukrainian strikes. On Friday, another Russian refiner suspended some crude oil operations, Reuters reported. NBC News has not verified the report. Additionally, a group of American lawmakers introduced a bill that would block Trump’s deal for Russian diesel. It has little chance of passing the Republican-controlled House. But polling indicates that Republicans are unlikely to maintain a majority in the House after November’s elections. The Russian diesel blocking bill offers a preview of the kind of legislation that could advance under Democratic control. Yet even now, the legislation adds to “growing doubts that a U.S. — Russia diesel deal will come to fruition,” said Mason Mendez, global real assets analyst at Wells Fargo. “Investors also remain concerned about further military escalation in the Middle East, as attacks on commercial shipping and regional infrastructure have increased in recent weeks,” he said. “Looking into 2027, the need to rebuild depleted global inventories could create an addition source of demand and keep energy prices elevated for longer.”

data.title: Elon Musk shows off ‘flying’ Tesla Roadster after years of delays
data.description: Elon Musk showed off the new Tesla Roadster prototype Thursday that can briefly launch itself into the air using rocket-inspired thrusters, nearly a decade after the electric sports car was first announced. The stunt-filled demonstration offered a glimpse of Tesla’s ambitious plans for the long-delayed vehicle. But the company has yet to announce a price or release date, and Musk, CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, said production would not begin until 2028 — eight years after the Roadster was originally expected to arrive. At a SpaceX testing facility in Texas, Musk told the live audience they were there to prove what they were about to see “was not AI or SI.” The vehicle, a collaboration between Tesla and SpaceX, then slowly drove up a curved ramp shaped like half of a rollercoaster loop before accelerating and launching itself off the ramp, hurdling over five other Tesla vehicles and bringing itself to a soft landing in a cloud of condensation using cold-gas thrusters. “Well, it worked!” Musk said after the stunt, adding that “it’s not necessarily a safety-optimized car.” Tesla says a fan-based suction system creates downforce to hold the vehicle against the road’s surface, while self-refilling cold-gas thrusters power its airborne maneuvers. He quipped, “This car really sucks.” Then the car accelerated toward the same five cars and jumped 27 feet in the air, according to Tesla, while performing a barrel roll and again brought itself down gently. Minutes later, it sped away with a 0.81-second 0-60 mph time according to Tesla, which is more than a second faster than the company’s current fastest time with the now-discontinued Model S Plaid.Tesla plans to offer three versions of the vehicle. The base Performance car will be “road-ready,” featuring the suction system but no thrusters, while the “race-ready” Thrust version will add rear-mounted thrusters for acceleration. The “air-ready” Rocket version will be invite-only, seat one person and contain the cold-gas thrusters along the perimeter of the car making it capable of the acrobatics shown in the live demonstration, according to Tesla. The flying features raise questions about where and how customers would be allowed to use the vehicle. Musk acknowledged the Roadster might not be legal in every jurisdiction, and Tesla says the Rocket version is not approved for public roads. The second-generation Roadster was first unveiled in 2017, with Musk initially promising production in 2020. The company has repeatedly pushed back that timeline while continuing to accept reservations from prospective buyers. Musk said when it releases, he wants it to “crack halfway to the speed of sound,” or about 383 mph, more than 150 mph faster than the current announced top speed. According to Musk, when it is released it will be able to go 300 miles on a single charge, less than half of what he had originally promised when he announced the car. No release date or price was revealed, but prospective buyers can reserve the base model for an initial deposit of $50,000 or $250,000 for the Thrust augment. Tesla says production will begin in 2028.

data.title: Brazil’s Lula wins electoral court challenge against Meta for alleged pro-Bolsonaro algorithm bias
data.description: SAO PAULO — A judge of Brazil’s top electoral court ruled Thursday that Meta must adopt measures to immediately secure equal treatment of the two presidential candidates ahead of an Oct. 25 runoff. The ruling comes shortly after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is running against Flávio Bolsonaro, filed a complaint that accused the tech company that owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp of using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favor opposition candidate Bolsonaro ahead of the election. Justice Marco Aurélio Bellizze ruled that Meta cannot reduce the distribution of political content, restrict searches or remove posts in a way that creates an imbalance between Lula and Bolsonaro. His ruling also orders the company to ensure its artificial intelligence tool applies identical criteria to both candidacies. Bellizze said in his ruling that Meta must pay a fine of 500,000 reais ($98,000) per day if it fails to comply. The legal filing of the Lula campaign, to which The Associated Press had access, said Meta has subjected Lula’s campaign materials and organic posts to “unjustified reductions in reach.” It also said Meta has not complied with a plan submitted to the electoral court to address these issues. Meta declined to comment on the ruling. Lula’s campaign argues that accounts and advertisements associated with Flávio Bolsonaro have reportedly received artificially inflated visibility, with engagement metrics rivaling those of global celebrities. The two are in a close race for the presidency, after the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro garnered 47% of the vote against 45% for the incumbent in the first round on Oct. 4. Lula’s complaint also claims there’s a stark disparity in Meta’s artificial intelligence tools, with users failing to generate campaign images related to the 80-year-old president via WhatsApp’s “Meta AI” feature, but being able to do so if they want to promote content in support of Flávio Bolsonaro. Gean Ferreira and Evelyn Santos, both lawyers for the Lula campaign, said in a statement that Meta’s content delivery is selective against the incumbent and favorable to Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump. “On one hand, content from candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and his supporters faces delivery restrictions, without any justification or transparency,” the lawyers said. “On the other hand, profiles acting as political operatives for the opposing side ... receive a disproportionate and artificial reach, garnering more views even than global celebrities.” Lula’s campaign wants Brazil’s top electoral court to order an immediate end to the content restrictions and pressure Meta to make up for the lost traction by doubling its reach to rectify the harm inflicted. On Oct. 11, as Lula’s voters started complaining about their use of Meta tools, the big tech company told the electoral court it rejects accusations of being skewed toward Bolsonaro. The company admitted it has faced technical glitches that affect accounts beyond Brazil. It also said it acts in full compliance with Brazil’s electoral regulations and is committed to providing equal platform access for all political parties.

data.title: Will the Fed raise interest rates this month? A Kevin Warsh speech could offer clues
data.description: When Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh strides onstage in Bangkok on Friday morning, it will be after 11 p.m. on Thursday in New York. But investors, economists and politicians in the United States will be awake and hanging on his every word. Any speech by a Fed chair is closely scrutinized. This week’s talk has an extra dose of urgency, though, after two government reports showed inflation heating up for consumers and businesses — spurring speculation about how soon the Fed will raise interest rates to handle soaring prices. Warsh will be speaking at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, where he will be interviewed by IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. The Fed chairman has repeatedly said he will not use public speaking engagements to intentionally steer the expectations of investors and markets, but his comments could nevertheless signal whether the central bank will hike rates before, or after, the Nov. 3 midterm elections. It will also be the last speech from a Fed official before policymakers enter a “blackout” period on Saturday that lasts through their next interest rate meeting, which is scheduled for Oct. 27 and 28. “Broad based” inflation “strengthens the case for an October hike,” Bank of America analysts wrote on Wednesday. “The data continue to underscore two key sources of inflation pressure: AI and Iran.” Those two factors aren’t likely to be going anywhere soon, either. The price of politics Already hammered by soaring interest rates, rising energy prices and stagnant wage growth, American consumers could get an extra dose of financial strain if the Fed raises rates again this month. Voters are already dissatisfied with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, polls show, so another rate hike could add to Republicans’ headaches as they face potentially losing their congressional majorities in the midterms. In recent weeks, Trump has tried to pull multiple policy levers to lower gas and diesel prices, which have pushed inflation higher in recent months. But none of them have yet slowed prices meaningfully. “Starting on day one, we will end inflation and make America affordable again,” Trump said on the campaign trail in 2024. Inflation as measured by the consumer price index declined to as low as 2.3% four months into Trump’s term. But that same month, Trump unleashed a wave of tariffs across the globe, dramatically changing the economic story. By September, inflation breached the 3% threshold again. In February, Trump launched the war against Iran, causing one of the worst energy supply shocks in history. Inflation jumped as high as 4.1% in May, and looks to be headed back in that direction again. Another Fed rate hike would also further undermine Trump’s yearslong pressure campaign to push the central bank to cut rates. Since Warsh took his post in May, the central bank has either held rates steady or increased them. Trump hasn’t attacked Warsh after years of hammering former Chair Jerome Powell. But the president has started saying that the other members of the Fed’s board are “very hostile.” “I’m relying on Kevin,” Trump told reporters in September, “but he’s got, you know, a very tough board. He’s got a board that was put there by a lot of other people, and the interest rates are too high.” “They’re very political,” Trump said. Four of the Fed’s seven board members were appointed by Trump. The White House did not immediately comment when asked what kind of expectations Trump has for Warsh’s appearance in Bangkok. Diesel and the damage done Economists and investors are paying close attention to so-called core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices. Both reports this week showed that even this adjusted measure of price growth is running hotter than hoped for. “Core CPI was the more significant surprise,” wrote analysts at Bank of America. The core readings showed that skyrocketing fuel prices, particularly diesel, are trickling down. Farmers, truckers and others who keep commerce humming in the United States have to raise their prices in order to digest higher diesel costs. That, in turn, leads to price increases for consumer goods. “The cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk told NBC News in an August interview. “Everything from … running a farm … cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped gets that extra fee tacked onto it.” At the time, she described the surge in diesel fuel prices as likely “an inflationary problem for the next several months.” Her warning came to fruition in September, according to the consumer price index and producer price index reports this week. With diesel prices remaining solidly above $6 per gallon so far in October, and with no sign that the Iran war is near an end or that attacks on energy assets in the Ukraine-Russia war will be paused, it could keep fueling overall inflation for months. Big Tech is also fueling inflation. Trillion-dollar companies are spending, and borrowing, big sums for servers, memory and other components that will be used in data centers. That’s caused price spikes across the economy. Companies including Apple and Nintendo have raised prices as a result. “We have never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly,” Apple told NBC News in June. Companies are also tapping the public debt markets in an unprecedented way. Data center companies and associated utility firms, chipmakers and cloud providers are expected to raise between $300 billion and $570 billion from the debt market this year, according to Vanguard. Those firms are also offering highly attractive interest rates, sometimes better than U.S. Treasury bonds. A consequence of that, Warsh noted recently, is that there’s a “competition for capital” driving up interest rates on government debt, too. “This is a complicated set of things that are affecting the most important asset anywhere in the world, the 10-year Treasury,” Warsh said. “It’s the risk-free asset upon which every price of virtually every asset in the world is related to.” Without referencing the Iran war, he also said yields were being driven by “geopolitics” and the strength of the economy.

data.title: Cracks are beginning to show in the stock market, as doubts grow about AI investments
data.description: Just one week after hitting fresh all-time highs, U.S. stocks are showing signs of strain as investors begin to fret about returns on the trillions of dollars that have been put into AI. For U.S. consumers, it could mean a shakier economy moving forward. As of Thursday morning, the S&P 500 was off more than 1% from its week-ago record, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq had fallen about 4% below its peak last week. Driving the declines: Quarterly revenue growth at Anthropic has slowed, the Financial Times reported Wednesday. The AI giant is expected to be worth more than $1 trillion when it goes public, and at nearly $17 billion, its revenue is still massive and the company said it is profitable. There are also rising concerns about whether China-based memory technology companies could undermine, or even overtake, their Western rivals. And even though the AI data center buildout has created a global shortage of processing chips, there are fears that Chinese mass production of memory chips could flood the market with an oversupply. Meanwhile, investors have begun selling off the bonds backing some data centers, primarily over fears that AI revenues won’t be sufficient to cover the massive sums that have been borrowed to finance the centers’ build-outs. On Thursday, economist Ed Yardeni, a widely respected market commentator, lowered his year-end target for the S&P 500 target to 7,900, down from 8,400, over what he said was rising investor caution about the AI trade and lingering doubts about inflation and higher interest rates. The S&P 500 currently sits at about 7,600. Most Americans don’t directly own tech stocks, let alone work in AI, which a growing number of studies show may have begun to limit job opportunities. Still, the AI buildout has been a massive part of what’s bolstering the economy, at least on paper. Nearly half of all U.S. economy growth this year is attributable to tech-related spending. Those investments have also lifted the stock market even as a growing swath of other companies have experienced sharp declines in their share prices. The tech-driven gains have in turn created a wealth effect that has helped propel steady U.S. consumer spending, and by extension the job market. The result has been sturdy economic growth, even as lower and even middle-income households have continued to struggle under stubborn inflation and declining earnings. “While higher interest rates, higher oil prices and persistent inflation create risks to the economy, strong positive forces such as the investment in AI infrastructure, high employment levels and consistent wage growth continue to outweigh the risks,” Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf said earlier this week. But other economists say consumers are already contending with a host of stressors that stand to weaken their position. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Thursday that inflation among businesses reached its highest rate since December 2022 — price-growth that could eventually trickle down to consumers. If tech spending — and stocks — show any sign of sustained declines, broader U.S. economic growth would likely be at risk. “Higher interest rates, elevated energy prices, slow job growth and the sell-off in equities (if it continues) are all downside risks to consumer spending,” analysts with Citi wrote in a note Thursday.

data.title: Businesses were hit even harder by inflation last month than consumers
data.description: Businesses were hit by inflation last month at levels not seen since late 2022. The latest U.S. wholesale inflation report showed that prices paid by businesses to produce goods in September jumped sharply, to 6.3% on an annual basis. From August, prices overall rose 0.6%, the Producer Price Index report showed. The PPI report is typically seen as a sign of what’s to come for consumer prices, and this one followed a Consumer Price Index report Wednesday which also reflected a jump in prices. Both reports indicate that inflation is back on the rise. But unlike high inflation earlier this year, the current impacts of rising prices are distributed broadly across the entire economy — beyond merely those sectors exposed to soaring gas, diesel and jet fuel prices. The consumer and producer price indexes are also the last major inflation readings before voters across the country head to the polls in the midterm elections. At many locations, early voting is already underway. Oil and gas prices have soared ever since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February. “Half of the September increase” in producer prices was from the rising cost of gas, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said Thursday . Likewise, prices for “diesel fuel, fresh and dry vegetables, jet fuel, residential electric power, and crude petroleum also rose.” Economists say that the most troubling recent price hikes have been those for diesel. Diesel fuel is critical to powering the farming, transportation and shipping sectors. When diesel prices go up, the knock-on effects of those higher costs can show up in just about every sector of consumer goods. Months of efforts by the Trump administration to bring down prices have failed to make a meaningful dent in rising costs. All of the key numbers in Thursday’s PPI report were far more than had been expected by economists and analysts. So-called “core” PPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, jumped 0.7% from August. From this time one year ago, it rose 5%. The report reinforced some market expectations that the Federal Reserve could hike interest rates sooner than expected, during its October 27-28 meeting. A rate hike would add more pressure to consumers, who are already facing high borrowing costs due to rising bond yields. The average interest rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage Thursday was 7.45%. Bond yields fell sharply Thursday in early trading, although this was primarily because investors were seen as moving out money of interest rate-sensitive tech stocks and into bonds. Tech stocks have become highly sensitive to interest rates in recent years because the top players are spending hundreds of billions of dollars — much of it borrowed with interest — to build data centers around the world.

data.title: Israeli ad company helped a spyware firm target Al Jazeera through online ads, researchers say
data.description: An Israeli ad company, DiscoverTech, has for years been secretly helping spyware developers place their hacking software on popular websites, researchers at Citizen Lab say, resulting in a cyberattack that targeted at least 45 devices at the news outlet Al Jazeera. The findings, documented in a report published Thursday by Citizen Lab, are the first time cybersecurity experts have shown how online ad platforms, so common across the internet that they are inescapable, can be used as a vector to hack visitors’ devices without their knowledge. “Any time we browse the internet or open an app, all the data on our device can be hacked by malicious actors without us even knowing,” said Natalia Krapiva, a spyware expert at the digital rights nonprofit Access Now, who read the report and was not involved with its research. “States and tech companies whose infrastructure is used to conduct these attacks need to take urgent technical, legal and regulatory measures.” The report is a joint effort between Confiant, a U.S. ad security company, and the Citizen Lab, a University of Toronto operation that researches mercenary spyware computer programs. Spyware is often leased to governments around the world to help them hack devices of people they want to spy on. While spyware companies often tout their products as crucial tools for governments to enforce national security, the tech has repeatedly been used around the world to crack down on journalists, human rights advocates and political opposition. DiscoverTech is a Tel Aviv company that sells online advertising services, the report said. “We take pride in providing our clients with a gateway to global fraud-free traffic, connecting your brand with real users,” its site says. DiscoverTech is one of a number of companies that help brands show their advertisements on websites that may be visited by potential customers. But the company secretly ran a separate program, the report says, that allowed spyware companies to inject malicious software onto visitors’ devices. The malicious code used to hack Al Jazeera computers was particularly effective, the researchers said, because it was “no-click” spyware — meaning a victim did not need to download a file or even click a link to be infected, just visit a website with a vulnerable computer and see the ad. The hacks, which were not previously reported until the release of the Citizen Lab’s report, occurred in 2024 and 2025. Al Jazeera provided the Citizen Lab with network logs from the period of the attacks, which researchers used to reconstruct how they unfolded, the Citizen Lab said in the report. It previously reported that the phones of 36 Al Jazeera journalists and staff members had been hacked with what it said was Pegasus spyware made by a different Israeli company, NSO Group, most likely by operators linked to Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. NSO said at the time that it would review the findings. Al Jazeera did not respond to a request for comment. Neither did DiscoverTech and its CEO. Like many advertising platforms, DiscoverTech has a wide reach: The report said it serves ads on almost 200,000 websites, Android apps and iOS apps, including those of major media organizations, search engines, government agencies and dating services. The report says Confiant detected DiscoverTech ads served on networks of major government entities like those of the U.S. Defense Department and the Dutch Economic Affairs Ministry, though it emphasized that the presence of ads does not indicate those organizations were targeted in malicious campaigns. Five ad vendors and industry organizations responded to the Citizen Lab’s findings by disconnecting DiscoverTech from their platforms. A Google spokesperson told NBC News that Google had helped the Citizen Lab and Confiant in their investigation and affirmed their findings, saying DiscoverTech is now banned on Google Ads. A spokesperson for IAB Europe, the continent’s largest trade organization for the advertising industry, said it has suspended DiscoverTech from its platforms. The report said the ad platforms Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi took similar action. The online advertising industry is a vast, convoluted and largely unregulated system that relies on maintaining significant technical information about people. Websites rarely directly control which companies post ads on their sites. Instead, advertisers preprogram “bids” for every person who visits and often prefer to advertise to people matching certain characteristics so their ads can be more targeted. The industry usually refrains from collecting specific personal information on people, but it assigns them industry “advertising IDs” and ties information like age, sex, location and preferences to them. The researchers say DiscoverTech taps into that system to offer a secret program called Controlium, which allows spyware companies to use DiscoverTech’s ad network to identify people to hack and help them deliver the malicious code to take over their devices. Controlium is not mentioned on DiscoverTech’s website, but researchers say they found source code on its login pages and were able to view aspects of how the program works. It allowed users to pick specific people to infect or profile using their phones’ advertising IDs, browser identifiers or IP addresses, numbers assigned to internet connections that can help tie people to locations such as their homes. The researchers found that Candiru, an Israeli spyware company that now operates as Integrity Labs, used DiscoverTech’s ads to deliver its spyware. The U.S. Commerce Department added Candiru to its Entity List in 2021, saying foreign governments had used its software to target journalists, activists and government officials. Wolfie Christl, one of the Citizen Lab researchers behind the report, said it illustrates something cybersecurity experts have long warned about: that the murky online advertising industry can be a vector for hackers to target victims and that most people should consider ad blocking software to be an essential cybersecurity tool. But even that is not foolproof, he said. “I think that our findings confirm once again that ad blocking must be considered a cybersecurity best practice. However, as ad blockers often try to balance protection and usability, they might still not consistently protect from malicious ads and other malicious code,” Christl said. “We recommend resetting or disabling the so-called Advertising ID on mobile devices and using opt-out features of apps. Generally, it’s difficult, if not almost impossible, to consistently protect yourself from malicious ads,” he said.
